name: Heart Rate
howToMeasure: Measured using the onboard wrist-worn bio-monitor or chest-strap heart rate sensor. Astronauts should remain seated and relaxed for at least 2 minutes before taking a resting measurement. The sensor continuously tracks BPM and can also detect arrhythmias.
whyItMatters: Heart rate is a fundamental indicator of cardiovascular health. In microgravity, the heart undergoes structural remodeling — it becomes more spherical and can lose muscle mass. Monitoring resting heart rate helps detect early signs of cardiovascular deconditioning, autonomic dysfunction, and stress responses.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity causes fluid redistribution toward the head, increasing cardiac preload and potentially leading to elevated resting heart rate. Prolonged microgravity exposure causes cardiac atrophy and reduced stroke volume. Radiation exposure can damage cardiac tissue. Psychological stress from isolation further elevates resting heart rate.

name: Blood Pressure (Systolic)
howToMeasure: Measured using the automated oscillometric blood pressure cuff in the medical kit. The astronaut should sit with arm at heart level (relative to body in microgravity), remain still, and take three readings spaced 1 minute apart. Record the average.
whyItMatters: Systolic blood pressure reflects the force exerted on arterial walls during heartbeats. Sustained hypertension accelerates cardiovascular disease, increases risk of stroke, and can worsen spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). Hypotension can cause fainting, especially dangerous during EVAs or re-entry.
hazardEffect: Microgravity causes cephalad fluid shift, initially raising intracranial and upper-body blood pressure. Over time, total blood volume decreases by 10-15%, and orthostatic intolerance develops. Upon return to gravity, astronauts are at high risk of syncope. Radiation exposure may damage blood vessel endothelium.

name: Blood Pressure (Diastolic)
howToMeasure: Measured simultaneously with systolic pressure using the automated oscillometric blood pressure cuff. Follow the same protocol — sit still, arm at heart level, three readings averaged. Diastolic is the lower number.
whyItMatters: Diastolic pressure indicates the pressure in arteries when the heart rests between beats. Elevated diastolic pressure puts chronic stress on the cardiovascular system and can indicate arterial stiffness. Low diastolic pressure may reduce coronary perfusion, risking ischemia.
hazardEffect: Spaceflight-induced blood volume reduction and cardiac deconditioning alter diastolic pressure regulation. The baroreceptor reflex becomes blunted in microgravity. Combined with arterial stiffening from radiation-induced endothelial damage, diastolic dysregulation becomes a significant concern on long-duration missions.

name: Blood Glucose
howToMeasure: Measured using the portable glucometer in the medical kit. Clean the fingertip with an alcohol swab, prick with the lance, and apply a drop of blood to the test strip. Fasting glucose should be measured in the morning before breakfast for the most reliable reading.
whyItMatters: Blood glucose levels reflect metabolic health and energy regulation. Hypoglycemia impairs cognitive function, coordination, and decision-making — all critical during spaceflight operations. Hyperglycemia indicates insulin resistance or dietary issues and increases infection risk, wound healing problems, and long-term organ damage.
hazardEffect: Spaceflight disrupts circadian rhythms that regulate glucose metabolism. Reduced physical activity in microgravity promotes insulin resistance. The stress of isolation elevates cortisol, which raises blood glucose. Pre-packaged space food may have suboptimal glycemic profiles. Radiation exposure can damage pancreatic beta cells.

name: Body Temperature
howToMeasure: Measured using the tympanic (ear) infrared thermometer or the skin-contact forehead sensor integrated into the bio-monitor headband. For accuracy, measure at the same time daily and avoid measurement immediately after exercise. The continuous-wear thermal patch provides 24-hour monitoring.
whyItMatters: Core body temperature regulation is essential for enzyme function, immune response, and neurological health. Fever indicates infection or inflammation. Hypothermia impairs judgment, motor function, and cardiovascular stability. In the closed spacecraft environment, an undetected infection could become a crew-wide emergency.
hazardEffect: Spaceflight causes a phenomenon called 'space fever' — astronauts' core temperature rises by about 1°C over months in microgravity due to impaired convective heat loss. The closed environment limits natural thermoregulation. Radiation-induced immune suppression makes astronauts more susceptible to infections that cause fever.

name: Sleep Duration
howToMeasure: Tracked automatically by the wrist-worn actigraph sensor that monitors movement patterns and heart rate variability during sleep. Astronauts also self-report sleep quality and duration in the morning health check. The crew quarters light sensor confirms lights-out and wake times.
whyItMatters: Adequate sleep is critical for cognitive performance, emotional regulation, immune function, and physical recovery. Sleep deprivation impairs reaction time, decision-making, and spatial awareness — skills essential for spacecraft operations, EVAs, and emergency responses. Chronic poor sleep accelerates bone loss and muscle atrophy.
hazardEffect: Spaceflight severely disrupts sleep due to 16 sunrises per day on the ISS (90-minute orbits), absence of natural light-dark cues, noise from life support systems, and the discomfort of sleeping in microgravity. Isolation and confinement increase anxiety, further degrading sleep quality. Studies show ISS astronauts average only 6 hours per night.

name: Mood Score
howToMeasure: Self-reported on a 1-5 scale during daily check-ins: 1 = Very Low (distressed), 2 = Low (struggling), 3 = Neutral (okay), 4 = Good (positive), 5 = Excellent (thriving). Astronauts are encouraged to add free-text notes about contributing factors.
whyItMatters: Psychological well-being directly impacts crew cohesion, decision-making, motivation, and mission success. Persistent low mood can indicate depression, which is associated with immune suppression, appetite changes, and increased error rates. Early detection allows ground-based psychologists to intervene with cognitive behavioral strategies.
hazardEffect: Isolation from family and society, confinement in a small habitat, interpersonal friction with crewmates, communication delays with Earth (up to 24 min one-way to Mars), monotony of routine tasks, and the existential weight of being far from home all contribute to psychological stress and mood deterioration.

name: Blood Oxygen Saturation
howToMeasure: Measured using the finger pulse oximeter clipped to the fingertip. The sensor uses infrared light to measure oxygen saturation in the blood. Take the reading after sitting still for 1 minute. The wrist bio-monitor also provides continuous SpO2 tracking via photoplethysmography.
whyItMatters: SpO2 indicates how effectively the lungs are oxygenating the blood. Values below 90% constitute hypoxemia, which can cause confusion, shortness of breath, rapid heart rate, and organ damage. In the closed spacecraft environment, SpO2 changes may also indicate cabin atmosphere problems (O2 level drops, CO2 buildup).
hazardEffect: The closed spacecraft environment requires precise atmospheric management. CO2 scrubber malfunctions can reduce available oxygen. Microgravity alters pulmonary ventilation-perfusion matching, potentially reducing gas exchange efficiency. Fluid shift to the upper body can cause mild pulmonary edema. Dust particles on the Moon and Mars pose inhalation risks.

name: Body Weight
howToMeasure: In microgravity, weight is measured using the Space Linear Acceleration Mass Measurement Device (SLAMMD), which calculates mass based on Newton's Second Law by applying a known force and measuring acceleration. Measurements are taken weekly at the same time of day while wearing standard clothing.
whyItMatters: Body weight changes reflect overall nutritional status, muscle mass maintenance, and fluid balance. Astronauts typically lose 1-5% of body weight during spaceflight due to muscle atrophy, bone demineralization, and appetite suppression. Rapid weight loss may indicate inadequate nutrition, dehydration, or illness.
hazardEffect: Microgravity unloads bones and muscles, leading to atrophy. Astronauts lose approximately 1-2% of bone mineral density per month and can lose up to 20% of muscle mass on long missions without countermeasures. Altered taste perception and appetite suppression in space often lead to reduced caloric intake, accelerating weight loss.

name: Daily Exercise Duration
howToMeasure: Tracked by the exercise equipment's built-in sensors (ARED resistance device, CEVIS cycle ergometer, T2 treadmill). Session duration, intensity, and heart rate are logged automatically. Astronauts follow a prescribed exercise protocol: approximately 2.5 hours of combined resistive and aerobic exercise daily.
whyItMatters: Exercise is the primary countermeasure against bone loss, muscle atrophy, and cardiovascular deconditioning in space. The ISS exercise protocol has been shown to reduce bone mineral density loss from 2% to 0.5% per month. Exercise also improves mood, sleep quality, cognitive function, and immune response.
hazardEffect: Without gravity providing constant mechanical loading, bones and muscles rapidly deteriorate. Astronauts must perform intensive daily exercise to simulate gravitational loading. Equipment limitations, schedule pressures, fatigue, and injury can reduce exercise compliance, accelerating deconditioning.

name: Hydration Level
howToMeasure: Self-assessed on a 1-5 scale: 1 = Severely Dehydrated (dark urine, headache, dizziness), 2 = Dehydrated (dark yellow urine, thirst), 3 = Adequate (light yellow urine, no thirst), 4 = Well Hydrated (pale urine, no symptoms), 5 = Optimally Hydrated (clear urine, energized). Urine color chart provided for reference.
whyItMatters: Proper hydration is essential for kidney function, thermoregulation, cognitive performance, and cardiovascular stability. Dehydration impairs blood volume, increasing heart rate and reducing exercise capacity. It also concentrates urine, raising the risk of kidney stones — a serious concern in space where surgical intervention is limited.
hazardEffect: Spaceflight promotes dehydration through multiple mechanisms: the cephalad fluid shift triggers diuresis, reducing total body water by 10-15%. The dry cabin atmosphere (typically 25-40% humidity) increases insensible water loss. Altered thirst perception in microgravity means astronauts often don't feel thirsty despite being dehydrated. Water recycling systems may produce water with slightly altered taste, reducing intake motivation.
